Top three research-backed reasons to oppose a nationwide carbon tax:  
1) It would be regressive in practice—distributional studies show carbon pricing raises household energy and transport costs disproportionately for low- and middle-income families unless complex, politically fragile rebates are added.  
2) It risks harming U.S. competitiveness and jobs—industry and trade analyses warn higher energy and input costs will pressure energy‑intensive manufacturers, encouraging offshoring or shutdowns unless costly exemptions or border adjustments are adopted.

Good evening—let me be blunt: a nationwide carbon tax would act like a new tax on working families and U.S. manufacturers, not a dependable climate solution. Distributional studies show carbon pricing raises household energy and transport bills disproportionately for low‑ and middle‑income families unless complex, politically fragile rebates are layered in; industry and trade analyses warn higher energy and input costs will pressure energy‑intensive plants and risk offshoring unless costly exemptions or border adjustments are adopted; and climate‑economy models themselves show outcomes hinge on price levels, leakage, and carve‑outs—while targeted tools (innovation funding, standards, infrastructure) can cut emissions without adding a new tax on paychecks.
